title: Third-Party JavaScript Is Part of Your Attack Surface: Lessons from a Recent Supply-Chain Attack
summary: Third-party JavaScript supply chain vulnerabilities expose modern web application attack surfaces
detailed: In a recent incident, visitors to websites run by some of the world’s best-known brands, including news publishers, banks, airlines, and software companies, were served malicious JavaScript.
The code came through a script they had deliberately chosen to trust, delivered by a widely used third-party web service.
That is why a third-party supply-chain compromise is different from an application compromise.
QID 150545 – JavaScript Library Loaded via External Server reports out-of-scope JavaScript libraries found during crawling, including the page, library version, and external URL.
sentences: In a recent incident, visitors to websites run by some of the world’s best-known brands, including news publishers, banks, airlines, and software companies, were served malicious JavaScript.
Most of those organizations never deployed bad code.
The code came through a script they had deliberately chosen to trust, delivered by a widely used third-party web service.
The attackers did not break into those websites.
Instead, they exploited a weakness in the vendor’s platform to gain administrative control of some customer accounts, then modified the JavaScript those customers delivered through the vendor.
The vendor’s CDN served the altered code to every visitor of an affected page.
The lesson extends beyond one vendor: modern websites run code their owners did not write and often do not track.
That is why a third-party supply-chain compromise is different from an application compromise.
The attack did not require any change to the affected organizations’ source code, servers, or pipelines.
The malicious file was served from the vendor’s own CDN, with the vendor’s valid certificate, from a host every affected site already trusted.
Code review and server-side monitoring had nothing to catch.
One weakness in a shared platform reached many organizations in a single day.
Content Security Policy (CSP) tells the browser which sources may load scripts and receive data.
In this incident, the injected code loaded its main payload from an attacker-controlled domain, so a strong CSP could block it.
But much depends on the word strong.
Most affected sites had either no CSP or one that still let the payload run.
Allowlisting the vendor’s domain made no difference, because the malicious code came through that host.

Protection came from a restrictive script-src that did not allow the attacker’s domain. ‘unsafe-eval’ let an inline fallback copy of the payload run, and ‘strict-dynamic’ extended trust to scripts the compromised snippet inserted.
A tight connect-src limited exfiltration but could not stop wallet-address swapping inside the page.
These practices apply to any organization that runs external JavaScript on its website.
QID 150206 – Content-Security-Policy Not Implemented flags applications that send no CSP header, which leaves no browser-enforced limit on where scripts can load from.

QID 150207 – Content Security Policy Insecure Configuration flags weak elements: ‘unsafe-inline’, ‘unsafe-eval’, wildcard sources, a missing default-src, and missing or invalid reporting configuration.
This incident showed the effect of one of these directly, when ‘unsafe-eval’ let the inline payload run.
A QID 150207 finding does not mean a given policy would have allowed this particular attack.
That depends on the full policy, including script-src, trusted sources, and nonces or hashes.
Treat these findings as starting points for a policy review.
The vendor’s first investigative recommendation was to review CSP violation reports, and sites without reporting had none to review.
QID 150545 – JavaScript Library Loaded via External Server reports out-of-scope JavaScript libraries found during crawling, including the page, library version, and external URL.
It does not judge whether a library is malicious.
Its value is visibility: an inventory of external scripts is the basis for deciding which vendors to trust and which hosts a CSP should allow.
We have released QID 533507 – Known Malicious Script Reference Detected.
This unauthenticated check sends an HTTP GET request and inspects the response body for a script src referencing known malicious scripts.
Use it to inventory which applications load known malicious scripts and to prioritize the applications handling payments or cryptocurrency for CSP review.
TotalAppSec shows where you are exposed and how well your controls are configured.
Qualys Web Malware Detection asks a different question: is malicious content present?

Qualys Web Malware Detection combines heuristic analysis (signature rules for patterns such as encoded JavaScript); behavioral analysis (visiting the site with a vulnerable browser and watching for unexpected file writes or processes); reputation checks of pages, referenced URLs, and remotely loaded resources against public blacklists; and antivirus scanning of downloaded scripts and files.

Three detections relate directly to third-party script risk:
Reputation-based detection depends on a domain being blacklisted at scan time.
Attacker infrastructure is often new: Report URI found this campaign’s primary domain was registered the morning the attack began.
Continuous scanning, alongside preventive controls such as CSP, is paramount for that reason.
Together, these findings give three different views.
A script reference (QIDs 533507, 150545) shows where you depend on someone else.
A weak control (QIDs 150206, 150207) shows how much damage a compromised dependency could do.
Malicious content (QIDs 207003, 208000, 208001) is evidence that something harmful is present.
Follow the actions in the vendor’s report.

Confirm which pages ran the snippet during the exposure window, review CSP violation reports and outbound requests against the published indicators of compromise, and keep your web, CDN, and CSP logs.
The vendor and Report URI published different indicators, so check both.
The incident here did not require breaching a single customer’s application.
It required one weakness in a platform those applications trusted.
Securing a web application means having visibility into both the code you write and the external scripts you allow to run in your users’ browsers.
Qualys TotalAppSec and Web Malware Detection help you inventory those dependencies, check the controls that limit their impact, and find malicious content.
